tldr: The authors propose GIFT, a framework that constrains intermediate visual features during training using three auxiliary tasks: geometry, affordance, and goal. Without requiring extra condition inputs at inference time, GIFT refines internal representations to be control-oriented, significantly boosting manipulation robustness against unseen environmental shifts and in real-world tasks.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of GIFT. Using intermediate visual tokens from a backbone that takes input images, language instructions, and robot states, three training-time losses are imposed: geometry alignment, object-centric affordance prediction, and instruction-grounded goal region prediction. The exact same framework applies to both VLA models (top) and WAM models (bottom).
overview:
Large vision-language-action models (VLAs) and video-prediction-based world-action models (WAMs) can handle rich visual semantics and dynamics. However, they share a common failure mode: vulnerability to environmental distribution shifts such as changes in viewpoint, background, or object placement. This stems from the "action-sufficiency gap." Relying solely on action prediction or pixel reconstruction losses fails to preserve control-critical structures in intermediate features—such as physical reachability or 3D geometric relations between objects and the end-effector—leaving representations distracted by control-irrelevant visual redundancy.

Rather than complicating the inference pipeline of policies, the authors focus on representation learning: "how to guide intermediate features during training." Specifically, they developed GIFT (Guided Intermediate Feature Training), which tasks intermediate features with predicting three complementary structures: Geometry (governing motion feasibility), Affordance (relative poses between the target and the end-effector), and Goal (identifying regions to manipulate). Crucially, GIFT does not feed auxiliary predictions into the action head as extra inputs. Instead, it refines intermediate features purely via backpropagation and discards all auxiliary heads at inference time.

Extensive evaluations were conducted across simulation benchmarks (LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, RoboCasa) and real-world robots (single-arm xArm7 and dual-arm ARX X5). Across distinct action paradigms—including direct-regression VLAs, direct-diffusion WAMs, and inverse-dynamics WAMs—GIFT consistently and substantially improved zero-shot robustness, showing dramatic performance gains particularly on articulated-object tasks and high-precision dual-arm assembly.
contributions: Identified the "action-sufficiency gap" (the mismatch between visual richness and control utility) common to both VLAs and WAMs, and established a unified principle of supervising intermediate features with geometry, affordance, and goals.

Instantiated GIFT across three distinct policy designs—direct-action VLA, direct-diffusion Fast-WAM, and predictive inverse-dynamics WAM—using the same objectives without altering each model's native action interface.

Demonstrated through ablations that internalizing structure purely via training-time losses (No-injection) outperforms feeding auxiliary predictions into the action head at inference time (Injection).

Achieved superior robustness over corresponding baselines across seven distribution shifts in LIBERO-Plus, dual-arm articulated tasks in RoboCasa, and severe lighting and layout perturbations on physical robots.

sections.heading: Visually Rich Yet Prone to Failure: Uncovering the Action-Sufficiency Gap
sections.summary: VLAs and WAMs struggle under environmental changes. At the root of this failure is the action-sufficiency gap: visual richness does not guarantee control success. This paper introduces GIFT, which imprints three control-oriented structures—geometry, affordance, and goals—into intermediate features, achieving high robustness while preserving the policy's base architecture.
sections.details:
In pursuit of general-purpose robot control, web-scale VLAs and predictive WAMs that simulate future environmental transitions have become dominant. However, these models often suffer drastic drops in success rate when minor changes occur in camera viewpoints, object layouts, backgrounds, lighting, or initial robot poses. VLAs trained solely on action regression easily pick up "shortcuts" like background textures or camera artifacts. Meanwhile, WAMs trained on pixel reconstruction focus heavily on visual appearance, losing the 3D structures and object semantics necessary for physical contact. The authors term this mismatch the "action-sufficiency gap."

Prior attempts to introduce auxiliary tasks relied on specialized model architectures or custom decoder heads, lacking a general principle applicable across different paradigms. To address this, the authors introduce GIFT (Guided Intermediate Feature Training), an architecture-flexible framework.

The core concept of GIFT is organizing the essential information needed for robotic manipulation into training-time constraints on intermediate representations: (1) Geometry governing physical feasibility, (2) Affordance encoding relative poses between instruction-relevant objects and the end-effector, and (3) Goals grounding manipulation regions. Instead of feeding these predictions directly into the action head, GIFT supervises shared intermediate visual tokens, internalizing control-relevant structures into the model without introducing any inference-time overhead.

captions.F1: Zero-shot evaluation results under seven distribution shifts on LIBERO-Plus. GIFT-VLA and GIFT-WAM-Fast consistently outperform baseline StarVLA-OFT and Fast-WAM across all shifts: camera viewpoint, robot initial pose, language phrasing, lighting, background, sensor noise, and layout.

sections.heading: How GIFT Differs from Prior Work: Training Intermediate Features Directly
sections.summary: This section reviews existing work on structured guidance for VLAs and predictive representation learning in WAMs, highlighting how GIFT sets itself apart. GIFT does not depend on custom inference interfaces or extra condition inputs, serving as a reusable intermediate representation learning principle across models.
sections.details:
### 2-A Vision-Language-Action Models (VLAs) and Structured Guidance
Recent VLAs have improved continuous control performance via flow matching, diffusion, and action chunking (predicting multiple future actions at once). However, pure action supervision provides no guarantee that spatial awareness or contact relationships will be retained in intermediate representations. While prior methods explicitly inject 3D representations, align with geometry teacher models, or introduce external visual affordance and reasoning prompts, they almost always depend heavily on specific decoder architectures.

### 2-B World-Action Models (WAMs) and Predictive Representation Learning
WAMs enhance control by predicting environmental dynamics. However, the objective of reconstructing RGB latents at the pixel level tends to overfit to fine visual appearances. While approaches learning coarse latent actions, predicting geometry and semantics jointly, or introducing mask- or slot-based object-centric representations have emerged, most designs still bottleneck the action module on prediction outputs.

### 2-C Key Distinctions of GIFT
The critical distinction lies in "where" and "how" structured knowledge is applied. Whereas methods like GuidedVLA design task-specialized decoders, GIFT supervises the intermediate visual tokens shared directly with the action generation pathway. Furthermore, unlike DreamVLA or DIAL, which use future predictions as explicit conditioning inputs to the action head, GIFT adopts a "No-injection" design by default (no auxiliary outputs are fed into the policy at inference time). This removes inference-time computational overhead and error propagation, directly proving that performance gains stem from improved representation quality itself.

sections.heading: The Design of GIFT: Supervising Intermediate Layers with Geometry, Affordance, and Goals
sections.summary: This section explains the formulation of GIFT and its specific loss functions. GIFT applies direction-scale decomposed alignment with a geometry teacher to shallow layers, and predicts object-centric 20-dimensional affordances and binary goal masks from deep layers, scaling across a VLA and two WAM variants.
sections.details:
### 3-A Problem Formulation and Overview
Given multi-view images $O_t$, a language instruction $l$, and proprioceptive states $s_t$, the policy predicts an action chunk $A_t$. From intermediate visual tokens $Z_t^{(r)}$ extracted from the backbone $\mathcal{E}_\theta$, lightweight heads predict geometry, affordance, and goal targets. Shallow layers ($r=6$) capture low-level spatial layout and receive geometry guidance, while semantically rich final layers ($r=-1$) handle affordance and goal predictions.

### 3-B Three Pillars of Structured Intermediate Guidance
- **Geometry Guidance**: Uses a frozen geometry foundation model (VGGT) as a teacher. To prevent training instability caused by feature scale disparities, visual feature vectors are decomposed into unit direction vectors and logarithmic scales. An angular alignment loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ang}}$ based on cosine similarity is applied to direction vectors, and an $\ell_1$ loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{scale}}$ is applied to scales. Their weighted sum forms the geometry loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{geo}}$. This embeds 3D spatial layout into visual tokens without requiring depth sensors or point clouds at inference.
- **Affordance Guidance**: Inspired by HumanEgo, this module describes spatial relations between instruction-relevant objects and the robot end-effector in an object-centric frame. With the first manipulated object designated as anchor $a$, each of $K$ slots is assigned a 20-dimensional vector containing a role ID, object pose relative to the anchor (3D position + 6D continuous rotation), end-effector pose relative to the object, and gripper state. An affordance decoder aggregates visual tokens using learnable queries, trained via a Smooth L1 loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{aff}}$.
- **Goal Guidance**: To ground target regions on image planes, a binary target mask $M_t$ is constructed for each camera view. An instruction-conditioned goal decoder predicts low-resolution masks, optimized with a combination of binary cross-entropy and soft Dice loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{goal}}$.

### 3-C Instantiations Across Different Policies
- **GIFT-VLA**: Based on a Qwen3-VL backbone and StarVLA-OFT. Geometry loss is applied to shallow layers, while affordance and goal tokens are placed in the final layer. The action head performs direct regression.
- **GIFT-WAM-Fast**: Built on Fast-WAM. The three guidance objectives are applied to current-frame video tokens. At inference, cached current-frame features are used to diffuse actions directly.
- **GIFT-WAM-IDM**: An inverse-dynamics model that denoises actions conditioned on predicted future video representations. Guidance is applied to current-frame representations similarly to Fast-WAM.

### 3-D Auxiliary Feature Injection (Injection vs. No-injection)
The framework allows comparing "Injection" (feeding predicted affordance and goal features as extra inputs to the action head) against "No-injection" (refining intermediate features solely via backpropagated loss gradients). Default GIFT uses No-injection, requiring neither the geometry teacher nor auxiliary decoders at test time.

captions.F3: Comparison between Injection and No-injection designs. In (a) and (c), predicted affordance and goal latent features are fed into the action head. In (b) and (d), guidance acts purely via gradient backpropagation into intermediate features during training, preserving the model's native action generation interface at inference.

sections.heading: Simulation Results: Strong Robustness Across Severe Distribution Shifts and Articulated Tasks
sections.summary: Experiments were conducted on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboCasa. While maintaining high performance in standard settings, GIFT achieved substantial score improvements under unseen environmental shifts (zero-shot transfer). Ablations confirmed the complementarity of all three guidances and the superiority of the No-injection design.
sections.details:
### 4-A/B Experimental Protocol and Implementation Details
Evaluations used standard LIBERO (4 suites, 10 tasks each), LIBERO-Plus (7 shift types covering viewpoints, lighting, and backgrounds), and RoboCasa (humanoid GR1 tabletop tasks: 18 pick-and-place, 6 articulated-object tasks). All models were trained purely on standard data and evaluated zero-shot under perturbed environments without fine-tuning.

### 4-C Main Results
- **LIBERO (Standard Setup)**: Even when baselines were near saturation (~97–98%), GIFT-VLA reached 97.9% (+1.3 points), GIFT-WAM-Fast reached 97.7% (+0.1 points), and GIFT-WAM-IDM reached 98.5% (+0.5 points), preserving or improving in-distribution performance.
- **LIBERO-Plus (Zero-Shot Robustness)**: Compared to baselines, GIFT-VLA improved from 75.0% to 79.6% (+4.6 points), GIFT-WAM-Fast jumped from 60.0% to 72.6% (+12.6 points), and GIFT-WAM-IDM rose from 82.6% to 87.8% (+5.2 points). Notably, WAM-Fast improved by over 20 points under robot initial pose shifts.
- **RoboCasa (Humanoid & Articulated Tasks)**: GIFT-WAM-Fast achieved an 83.6% average (+9.0 points over Fast-WAM), and GIFT-WAM-IDM achieved 82.3% (+8.4 points). Dramatic gains were observed on articulated tasks (opening doors and drawers): +21.3 points for GIFT-WAM-Fast and +24.6 points for GIFT-WAM-IDM.

### 4-D/E Ablations and Analyses
- **Q1 Contribution of Each Guidance**: While individual guidances improved performance, geometry excelled under viewpoint shifts, affordance under robot pose shifts, and goals under background/noise shifts. Combining all three achieved the best overall performance.
- **Q2 Injection vs. No-injection**: Operating without auxiliary feature injection (No-injection) outperformed feeding auxiliary tokens (Injection) into the action head: 79.6% vs. 76.7% on LIBERO-Plus and 61.4% vs. 58.6% on RoboCasa (both using GIFT-VLA). Well-structured representations make redundant conditioning unnecessary.
- **Q3/Q4 Visualizations of Features and Attention**: Depth and goal masks reconstructed from intermediate tokens showed high accuracy. Attention maps from action tokens to visual tokens remained consistently focused on manipulated objects and contact areas in GIFT, unlike the scattered attention seen in baselines.

captions.F4: Visualization of intermediate feature predictions for GIFT-VLA (top) and GIFT-WAM-IDM (bottom). Even under severe viewpoint and background changes, geometry predictions retain coherent spatial layouts, affordances accurately estimate relative end-effector poses, and goal masks precisely isolate target regions.
captions.F5: Comparison of attention maps from action tokens to visual tokens on LIBERO-Plus. While baselines (StarVLA-OFT, Fast-WAM-IDM) scatter attention across irrelevant background areas, GIFT-equipped models stay focused on manipulated objects (bowls, ketchup) and placement containers.

sections.heading: Real-World Robot Experiments: Completing Dual-Arm Precision Tasks Under Severe Disturbances
sections.summary: Using a single-arm xArm7 and a dual-arm ARX X5, four tasks were evaluated: color sorting, multi-tier rack placement, cabinet manipulation, and test-tube insertion. Under heavy real-world disturbances—such as rotating colored lights, tablecloth shifts, unseen distractors, and initial pose offsets—GIFT demonstrated far greater robustness than baselines.
sections.details:
### 5-A Hardware, Data Collection, and Annotation
- **Hardware Setup**: Evaluated on a single-arm UFACTORY xArm7 equipped with third-person and wrist cameras, and a dual-arm ARX X5 equipped with head and dual wrist cameras (all Intel RealSense sensors).
- **Data Collection and Annotation**: 100 teleoperated demonstrations per task (400 episodes total) were collected. Operator gloves were inpainted on half the dataset to reduce visual bias. Tracking masks (goal targets) were extracted using Grounding DINO and SAM2, while 6-DoF poses (affordance targets) were obtained using RGB-D depth and Orient Anything V2.

### 5-B/C Real-Robot Results and Robustness Evaluation
- **Clean In-Distribution Setup**: Across the four tasks, GIFT-VLA improved success rates from 35.0% to 57.5%, and GIFT-WAM-IDM jumped from 52.5% to 87.5%. In the high-precision dual-arm test-tube insertion task (Task 4), Fast-WAM-IDM succeeded only 2/10 times, whereas GIFT-WAM-IDM succeeded 8/10 times.
- **Severe Perturbation Tests**: Physical, non-synthetic perturbations were applied. For rack placement, a rotating colored lamp introduced aggressive chromatic shifts (Level 1), combined with an unseen patterned tablecloth (Level 2). For test-tube insertion, random distractor objects were scattered in the background (Level 1), and tube/rack orientations were rotated by 15–20 degrees (Level 2).
- Under these perturbations, baseline performance collapsed (StarVLA-OFT averaged 5.0%, Fast-WAM-IDM averaged 15.0%). In contrast, GIFT-VLA retained a 27.5% success rate and GIFT-WAM-IDM achieved 67.5%. Imprinting geometry and affordance into intermediate features allowed the policy to maintain accurate physical contact awareness despite drastic visual shifts.

captions.F8: Real-world robot experimental setups. (a) Single-arm UFACTORY xArm7 equipped with third-person and wrist cameras. (b) Dual-arm ARX X5 equipped with a head camera and dual wrist cameras. Both setups use parallel-jaw grippers as end-effectors.

sections.heading: Conclusion and Future Outlook: A Common Principle Bridging General Vision Knowledge and Robot Control
sections.summary: GIFT provides an architecture-flexible training framework that bridges the action-sufficiency gap by supervising intermediate features with geometry, affordance, and goals. Refining intermediate layers purely via training losses without feeding auxiliary outputs into action decoders proved remarkably effective across diverse policy families.
sections.details:
This work addressed the fundamental "action-sufficiency gap" in modern robot foundation models like VLAs and WAMs by directly supervising intermediate representations. Without modifying model-specific action decoders or requiring extra conditioning inputs at test time, GIFT internalizes control-critical physical and task structures through geometry alignment, object-centric affordance prediction, and goal-region reconstruction.

Through broad simulation and real-world experiments, GIFT consistently enhanced perturbation robustness and control precision across direct-action VLAs, direct-diffusion WAMs, and inverse-dynamics WAMs. Future work includes exploring wider varieties of guidance signals, scaling up to larger datasets, and improving guidance reliability under extreme perceptual collapse.

takeaways: Relying solely on action prediction or pixel reconstruction losses in VLAs and WAMs retains control-irrelevant visual redundancy, causing severe sensitivity to distribution shifts (the action-sufficiency gap).

Guiding intermediate features during training with Geometry (feasibility), Affordance (how to interact), and Goals (where to act) refines internal representations for control without requiring extra inputs at inference.
Internalizing structure purely via backpropagated losses (No-injection) achieves higher robustness and performance than explicitly injecting auxiliary predictions into the action head (Injection).
The representation learning principle generalizes across policy architectures (VLA and WAM) and action formulations (regression, diffusion, and inverse dynamics).
limitations: Under extreme sensor noise or micro-geometric variations, failures in geometry alignment can negatively impact downstream action generation through corrupted spatial representations.
When visually similar distractor objects are present, affordance slot assignments can become confused, occasionally causing the robot to grasp the wrong object.

GIFT requires detailed training annotations such as object masks and 6-DoF poses (or high-accuracy pseudo-labeling pipelines), resulting in higher data preparation costs than vanilla imitation learning.
